analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to ban congressional stock trading has sat in two House committees with no hearing or vote since January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependents from owning or trading individual stocks, securities, commodities, or similar investments [S2][S3]. They would have 90 days to sell those holdings or move them into an ethics-approved blind trust, where an independent trustee manages the assets without the member's knowledge [S2][S3]. Widely held investment funds, Treasury bonds, municipal bonds, and the federal retirement plan would still be allowed [S3]. Members would have to certify compliance to an ethics office, which would post the certificates online, and willful violators could face a civil penalty of up to $50,000 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want lawmakers making policy without a personal financial stake in the outcome. Members with few investments pay little, while members who currently hold large individual stock portfolios would have to divest.

how_it_helps.text: Bars members, their spouses, and dependents from owning or trading individual stocks, securities futures, commodities, and similar investments, closing a route by which lawmakers could personally profit from legislative decisions [S2][S3].
Requires divestiture within 90 days, either by sale or by placing assets in a qualified blind trust with an independent trustee who may not share information about the assets with the member [S3].
Mandates public disclosure: the supervising ethics office must post every member's certificate of compliance on a publicly accessible website [S3].
Attaches real consequences, including referral to the Attorney General and civil penalties up to $50,000, plus denial of tax deductions for losses on violating transactions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families, who would have to sell individual stocks or give up control of them to a blind trust within 90 days. Members with large stock portfolios bear the largest change.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The maximum civil penalty is $50,000, which is small compared with the value of many congressional portfolios and could be treated as a cost of doing business by a wealthy member [S3].
Enforcement runs through the ethics office referring cases to the Attorney General, who must bring suit in court, adding layers between a violation and any penalty [S3].
Blind trusts get up to six months to divest after being established, and spouses who receive investments as job compensation get extra time to sell, so full compliance can be delayed [S3].

The ban allows unlimited holdings in widely held funds and government bonds, so a member could still hold millions of dollars in broad-market index funds tied to companies the member legislates on [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: lawmakers give up the ability to pick individual stocks, and the public gets a concrete firewall against conflicts of interest. The design is reasonable but not airtight — the $50,000 penalty cap is modest for wealthy members, and the index-fund carve-out still leaves broad market exposure. On balance the compliance cost to members is small relative to the integrity gain for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 9, 2025 by Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick with three original cosponsors across both parties: Reps. Ocasio-Cortez (D), Mills (R), and Krishnamoorthi (D) [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on House Administration and the Committee on Ways and Means, with the Speaker to later decide which committee takes the lead [S5].
It has 14 cosponsors, 11 House Democrats and 3 House Republicans [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — has been recorded in the five-plus months since referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress, whose existing freedom to hold and trade individual stocks remains untouched while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress keeping their stock portfolios

sides.party_line_note: The bill is genuinely bipartisan: its four original sponsors split two Republicans and two Democrats, and its 14 cosponsors split 11 Democrats and 3 Republicans [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would force them to divest individual stocks or place them in blind trusts, ending a way officeholders can hold investments directly affected by their own work. As the group whose conduct is being restricted, their institutional interest runs against the bill, and the lack of committee action leaves their current position intact.

industries.industry: Widely held investment funds (index funds and fund managers)
industries.note: Members who must divest individual stocks would shift money into broadly held diversified funds, which remain permitted under the bill. This is a modest, lawful channel for compliance.

analysis.trajectory: Bans on congressional stock trading have been introduced repeatedly in recent Congresses with bipartisan sponsors, and versions have repeatedly stalled in committee without a floor vote. With only 14 cosponsors and no committee action five months after referral, the likely path is that this bill also dies quietly unless House leadership elevates it — for example by attaching it to a larger rules or ethics package.
